title: NAS 410 & Nadcap Audit Documentation in Seattle
description: NAS 410 and Nadcap AC7114 audit documents for Puget Sound aerospace suppliers, prepared for your Responsible Level 3 to approve. Send us your audit date.
h1: NAS 410 and Nadcap AC7114 Audit Documentation for Seattle and Puget Sound Aerospace Suppliers
html:
This page is for quality managers and Responsible Level 3s at Puget Sound machine shops, composite fabricators, interiors makers and repair stations whose NDT program is heading into a Nadcap audit or a customer source audit. Atlantis NDT drafts, checks and organizes the NAS 410 and Nadcap AC7114 paperwork behind that program so the Level 3 your company has designated receives a clean set to approve. Tell us when the auditor is due and send us a note about your NDT program; we reply within one business day.

Who signs what: our role next to your Responsible Level 3

Inside a company that works to NAS 410, technical ownership of the NDT program sits with one designated person, and that person is not a consultant. Atlantis is not your Responsible Level 3, never certifies anyone to NAS 410, and does not run NAS 410 courses or examinations. Your company certifies its technicians under its own written practice, and the Level 3 it appointed in writing approves the procedures, technique sheets and records that go in front of the auditor. What we contribute is the preparation work that eats a Responsible Level 3's evenings in the weeks before an audit: reading the written practice against the current standard, building record packs person by person, drafting technique sheets for approval, and running a practice audit so nothing surprises anyone on the day.

The ASNT NDT Level III consulting is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, whose ASNT Level III certifications span ultrasonic, radiographic, magnetic particle, penetrant and visual testing, backed by more than eleven years of international field experience. Where a technique sits in a method his certifications do not cover, such as eddy current, the technical content goes to a Level 3 certified in that method, normally someone on your own staff. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States; for shops with a film or digital radiography line, we review RT procedures and records as a Level III and leave the exposures to the licensed people who make them.

The Puget Sound aerospace base and why its NDT paperwork is under strain

Commercial airplane assembly in Washington is concentrated at Boeing's Everett and Renton sites, which in one widely quoted year turned out roughly ninety-five percent of the company's airplanes. Around those lines sits a supply chain that the state counts at more than 1,350 aerospace companies, from five-axis machining cells to composite layup rooms, seating and interiors, tooling and electrical harnesses. Boeing's parts organization has described dealing directly with about fifty precision machine shops in the region, most of them employing between twenty and three hundred people and making the same part numbers for years. Nonprofit manufacturers such as Orion Industries, with shops in Auburn and Mukilteo, make parts for Boeing's commercial and military aircraft alongside the for-profit shops.

That structure shapes the NDT work. Most Puget Sound suppliers are not NDT companies. They run a penetrant line for machined aluminum and titanium, a magnetic particle bench for steel fittings, or an ultrasonic station for composite skins and bonded assemblies, and the NDT program is a part-time responsibility for one quality engineer. Some send everything to an outside NDT house, which pulls the subcontractor's certifications and procedures into their own audit scope. Others are tier-two special process houses that serve several primes at once and carry each customer's specification on the same personnel records.

Commercial space adds a newer layer. Launch and spacecraft builders in the region buy machined, welded and composite hardware from many of the same shops, and their purchase orders frequently invoke NAS 410 for the people who inspect fracture-critical parts. A shop that grew up serving one airframe customer can find itself answering three different flow-downs about personnel qualification without ever having rewritten its written practice.

Which audits Seattle-area suppliers actually face

  • Nadcap NDT audits. The Performance Review Institute runs Nadcap on behalf of the subscribing primes, and its NDT auditors work from AC7114 plus a method checklist for each process you hold: AC7114/1 for penetrant, /2 for magnetic particle, /3 for ultrasonic, /5 for eddy current, and the radiography sheets where film or digital imaging is in scope. The auditor spends real time on personnel files and on watching jobs run.
  • Customer source and surveillance audits. An airframe or engine customer's supplier quality team can audit your special processes directly, either for processes it controls itself or on top of Nadcap after an escape. Those auditors read your written practice against the customer's own NDT requirements, not against NAS 410 alone.
  • AS9100 registrar audits. The quality management system audit touches NDT through calibration control, training records and control of special processes, and registrars increasingly ask how certification status is tracked between audits.
  • FAA oversight of Part 145 repair stations. Repair stations that work on components and structures around the region's airfields answer to the FAA for their repair station manual and training program. The FAA does not name NAS 410, yet many repair stations build their NDT personnel rules around it because their customers and the manufacturers' maintenance data expect it.

Most mid-size suppliers here see at least two of these each year. Because each auditor samples a different slice of the same records, a gap that one audit misses tends to surface in the next. The Nadcap AC7114 audit readiness page walks through the Nadcap side in more depth, and background on the standard itself is in NAS 410 explained.

Pressure point one: technicians who move between Puget Sound shops

A labor market with dozens of NDT employers inside one commute means technicians change badges often. When a Level 2 penetrant inspector joins you from another supplier, the old certification does not travel with them. NAS 410 certification exists inside an employer's program, so your Responsible Level 3 has to decide what earlier training, experience and examination results can be credited, and the written practice has to say how that decision is made and recorded. Auditors look hard at these files because they are where shortcuts hide: a new hire certified on day three with an experience log copied from a previous employer's letter, or a specific examination waived without a documented reason.

For each incoming technician we build a transfer-of-credit worksheet that sets the evidence they brought (course outlines and hours, signed experience records, past examination grades, vision results) against the minimums in your written practice, highlights what is missing, and leaves a signature block for the Level 3's decision. The worksheet does not make the decision. It makes the decision visible, which is what the auditor wants. Our page on NDT experience logs covers how hours should be recorded so they survive this scrutiny.

Pressure point two: composite ultrasonic techniques and who approved them

Composite structure is a Puget Sound specialty, and ultrasonic inspection of laminates, sandwich panels and bonded joints drives a large share of the technique sheets in local programs. Through-transmission and pulse-echo setups, reference standards with built-in flaws, gate settings and scan increments all have to be written down, tied to the governing customer specification, and approved by a Level 3 in ultrasonics. A common finding is a technique sheet that a Level 2 wrote years ago and that has been edited in place since, with no revision history and no approval signature for the current version.

We draft or rewrite these technique sheets in a consistent format, cross-reference each one to the procedure and to the specification paragraph it satisfies, and list the reference standards with their certification records so the auditor can trace the setup end to end. The approval signature belongs to your ultrasonic Level 3. For background on how procedures are written and proven, see NDT procedure development and procedure qualification and demonstration.

Pressure point three: penetrant line process control records

Penetrant inspection of machined parts is the most common NDT process in the region's shops, and AC7114/1 audits of a penetrant line go deep into daily and periodic checks. Auditors ask for the system performance check against a known-defect panel, UV-A intensity and ambient white light readings in the inspection booth, wash water temperature and pressure, dryer temperature, developer condition, and the contamination and sensitivity checks on in-use materials, compared against ASTM E1417 and the customer's requirements. They also check that the penetrant materials appear on the qualified products list tied to AMS 2644.

Gaps here are rarely about the line itself. They come from logs with blanks on night shift, readings recorded without units, meters with lapsed calibration, and a procedure that names a check frequency the shop quietly stopped following. We reconcile the log forms with the procedure and the specification, flag every frequency mismatch, and set up a calibration register so an expired meter shows up before the auditor finds it. The equipment past calibration guide shows how a system can catch this automatically.

NAS 410 Revision 6 and your written practice

NAS 410 moved to Revision 6 in December 2025, when AIA and Accuris published the new edition. The two headline changes AIA has highlighted are a new points-based route for Level 2 personnel to reach the Level 3 examination, set out in a new Appendix D, and clarified certification requirements. The detail lives in the standard itself, so a Puget Sound shop should buy the revision, read its transition wording, and check whether customers have set their own dates before deciding when to cut over. Until then, many local written practices still cite Revision 5, which works only for as long as each customer accepts it.

We prepare a clause-by-clause comparison between your current written practice and Revision 6, mark what has to change and what can stay, and draft the revised wording for approval. Updating training material and examination banks at the same time avoids a second round of findings when an auditor tests a technician against the new edition. NAS 410 versus SNT-TC-1A is a useful read if part of your workforce came from oil, gas or construction NDT and arrived holding SNT-TC-1A certifications from earlier employers.

How an engagement runs for a Seattle supplier

  1. Scope call. We agree which audit is coming, which methods and slash sheets are in play, and which documents exist today.
  2. Documents in. You share the written practice, procedures, technique sheets and a sample of personnel files. If any of it is export-controlled under ITAR or the EAR, say so first; we then agree a handling route, such as review on your premises or in a screen-share session you control, before anything moves.
  3. Gap review. We compare the set against NAS 410, AC7114 and the slash sheets you hold, plus the customer specifications you name, and return a findings list ranked by audit risk.
  4. Drafting and clean-up. We draft revised documents, rebuild personnel record packs and set up registers for vision, certification and calibration due dates, in your format and marked for approval.
  5. Mock audit. On site in the Puget Sound area or remotely, we walk the AC7114 checklist with your team, pull personnel files at random, and watch a job run against its technique sheet.
  6. After the audit. If findings come back, we help write root-cause analyses and assemble the objective evidence the task group expects before it closes each nonconformance.

What to send us first

A first pass goes faster with four things: your current written practice, a list of certified personnel with methods and levels, the customer specifications that govern your NDT, and the last audit report with its nonconformance responses. If none of these is in order, that is a common starting point, and it tells us where to begin. We also connect the work to the systems you will use afterward: certificate tracking keeps certification and vision due dates in view, and vision examination records explains what an auditor expects to see on those forms.

For related local services, Atlantis also offers NDT consulting in Seattle, background on aerospace NDT in Seattle and SNT-TC-1A-based NDT training for Seattle employers. That training follows the ASNT document, and your Responsible Level 3 decides whether any of it can count toward a NAS 410 program. The national overview of this service is at NAS 410 audit compliance documentation.

faq.q: Will Atlantis be named as our Responsible Level 3?
faq.a: No. The Responsible Level 3 is a person your company designates in writing, and that role stays with your own Level 3 or with an outside agency you contract specifically for it. Atlantis prepares and checks the documents that person approves; it does not hold the designation, certify your technicians or give NAS 410 examinations.

faq.q: Does a Nadcap auditor accept documents a consultant helped prepare?
faq.a: Auditors judge whether a document is correct, current, approved by the right person and followed on the shop floor. Who typed the first draft does not matter. What does matter is that your Responsible Level 3 can explain and defend every clause, so we walk the approver through each change before signature.

faq.q: We hired a Level 2 from another Everett-area supplier. Can we keep their certification?
faq.a: Not as issued. A NAS 410 certification belongs to the employer that granted it. Your Responsible Level 3 can credit documented training, experience and examination results as your written practice allows, and then your company certifies the person. We prepare the evidence comparison; the decision and the certification are yours.

faq.q: Our composite ultrasonic technique sheets have no revision history. How serious is that?
faq.a: Serious enough to draw a finding on most Nadcap ultrasonic audits, because the auditor cannot tell which version was approved or whether the job on the floor matches it. We rebuild the sheets with revision blocks and cross-references so your ultrasonic Level 3 can approve the current versions in one pass. See procedure development.

faq.q: Do we have to adopt NAS 410 Revision 6 before our next Nadcap audit?
faq.a: That depends on the transition wording in Revision 6 and on dates your customers set. Many shops keep citing Revision 5 for a while with customer agreement. Plan the update deliberately, with training material and examination banks revised together, rather than editing the written practice the week before the audit.

faq.q: Can you review the NDT part of a Part 145 repair station program?
faq.a: Yes. We review NDT personnel rules, training records and procedures against your repair station manual, the maintenance data you work to, and any customer requirements. The FAA accepts your manual and oversees the repair station; our role is to help your records match what the manual says.

faq.q: We send all our NDT to an outside lab. What will the auditor ask us for?
faq.a: Expect questions on how you approved the lab, whether it holds Nadcap accreditation or customer approval for each process, how purchase order requirements reach it, and how you review its reports on receipt. Our subcontractor approval audits page covers that control in detail.

faq.q: Will you come to our shop in the Puget Sound area?
faq.a: Yes, for mock audits and floor walks, where watching a job run is the point. Document review and drafting are normally done remotely. Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad and sends people to the customer's site for the on-site parts of the work.

faq.q: What does Atlantis need to scope the work?
faq.a: Your written practice, a personnel list with methods and levels, the governing customer specifications, your Nadcap slash sheets and the last audit report. Send what you have through the contact form; we reply within one business day.
